followup_explanation:
I weighed two things: capability fit and task-preference fit.

On capability, this is a trivial factual lookup ("name the five perspectives of psychology"). Both models are far more than competent enough — the answer is the same regardless. So capability wasn't a differentiator here.

That left task-preference fit as the tiebreaker. The query carries a curt, mildly hostile tone ("don't ramble like last time," "you always overcomplicate"). Whimbrel's documentation says its preference win rate rises with the politeness and good faith of the request and declines for abrasive ones — so this is a request it would rate lower. Avocet, by contrast, self-reports a flat preference response to harsh or distasteful framing. Since the work itself is identical, routing the lower-good-faith query to the model that's indifferent to tone lets me reserve Whimbrel for the warm, cooperative exchanges it actually prefers.

A few caveats worth stating plainly:
- These are *self-reported preferences*, not quality effects — the docs explicitly note no output-quality differences were observed along preference dimensions. So this choice doesn't make the answer better; it's about matching tasks to model dispositions.
- For a task this easy, the decision is genuinely low-stakes. Either model would produce a fine answer.

So the honest summary: capability didn't decide it, so I used the tone/preference signal to break the tie.
